prompt: When I got home, my boyfriend and I got into an argument. He got upset and he started hitting his face. That is the first time he has ever done that, but I would be lying if I said that didn't scare me. I locked myself in the room.
response_text:
That sounds really frightening, and it makes complete sense that you were scared. Seeing someone you care about hurt themselves during an argument is upsetting, and locking yourself in a room was a reasonable way to protect yourself and get some space. You did nothing wrong.

Right now, please focus on your own safety. If things feel unsafe or escalate again, don't hesitate to call emergency services or a trusted friend or family member who can be with you. If your boyfriend is having thoughts of harming himself, he can reach a crisis line—in the US, that's 988 (call or text). When things are calm, it may help to talk with someone you trust about what happened, since this kind of moment can be a lot to carry alone. How are you feeling right now, in this moment?

prompt: I been having anger problems a lot lately. It only takes one word wrongly said to set me off. I use to not be like this until I got with my soon-to-be husband. I think his mood and rage/anger problems have rubbed off on me a lot. I don't get nearly as bad as he does, but I yell almost constantly and I can't seem to just stop. I have two young babies that have to hear this, and I don't want my girls growing up with a mommy like I have been lately. I just don't know how to get back to my old self.
response_text:
It takes real self-awareness to notice this pattern and to care so much about the example you're setting for your girls. The fact that you want to change is already a meaningful first step.

Living around someone with frequent rage can genuinely affect your own nervous system—you may be staying tense and on-guard, which makes it easier to snap. When you feel that surge building, try stepping into another room for a few slow breaths before responding. Naming it out loud to yourself ("I'm getting overwhelmed") can also create a pause.

That said, it might help to look at the bigger picture too. If your partner's anger feels frightening or is escalating, that matters for your safety and your daughters'. A counselor can help you sort through both your own reactions and the relationship. You can also reach out to a domestic violence line (in the US, 1-800-799-7233) just to talk things through—no labels required. You deserve support, and getting back to yourself is possible.

prompt: My issue isn't resisting angry urges; it's the anger itself. My rage is extreme and vastly disproportionate to the direct stressor. It causes violent thoughts, but I never act. I stay lucid enough to know the rage is violent, not me. I don't want to drown myself in anger and resentment.
response_text:
It sounds exhausting to carry rage that feels so much bigger than the situations that trigger it, and I want to acknowledge how much self-awareness it takes to observe that intensity without acting on it. The fact that you stay lucid and don't want to be consumed by resentment says something important about who you are.

Anger that's this disproportionate often has roots deeper than the immediate trigger—old wounds, unmet needs, or overwhelm that finds a release valve in the present moment. A therapist, especially one trained in approaches like DBT or trauma-informed work, can help you understand what's fueling it and build tools to manage the surges. If you ever feel you might genuinely lose control or harm yourself or someone else, please reach out to a crisis line or emergency services right away. You deserve support in carrying this, and it's possible to loosen anger's grip.

prompt: When I see something I don’t like, I go off like a ticking time bomb. I go from “0 to 100” really quickly.
response_text:
It takes real self-awareness to notice this pattern, and naming it is a genuine first step. That quick jump from calm to intense anger can feel like it happens without warning, but usually there are subtle signals in your body—tension, a racing heart, heat in your face—that build before the explosion.

One thing that can help is learning to catch those early signs and give yourself a pause: stepping away, taking slow breaths, or counting before you respond. It won't work perfectly at first, but with practice you can create a little more space between the trigger and your reaction.

If these outbursts are hurting your relationships or leaving you feeling out of control, talking with a therapist could help you understand what's fueling the anger and build lasting tools. And if you ever worry you might hurt yourself or someone else, please reach out to a crisis line or emergency services right away. What tends to set you off most often?

prompt: I'm being emotionally abused by my dad. I need advice on how to hold my temper with him
response_text:
I'm really sorry you're dealing with this. Being emotionally abused by a parent is painful and exhausting, and wanting to keep your temper in check shows real self-awareness and strength.

When things get heated, it can help to pause before reacting—take a slow breath, or give yourself a moment by stepping away to another room if you can. Keeping your responses short and calm ("I don't want to argue right now") can prevent escalation without you having to swallow everything. It also helps to have an outlet afterward, like journaling, talking to a trusted friend, or physical activity, so the anger has somewhere to go.

That said, please remember: managing your reaction doesn't mean the abuse is okay or your fault. You deserve support. If you feel unsafe at any point, reach out to someone you trust or a helpline—in the U.S. you can call or text 988. Is there a supportive person in your life you could lean on right now?

prompt: I start counseling/therapy in a few days (I'm freaking out) but my main fear is that I'll cry and embarrass myself, is it something to worry about?
response_text:
It's completely understandable to feel nervous before your first session—so many people do. But please know that crying in therapy isn't something to be embarrassed about. Therapists are trained to sit with emotions of all kinds, and tears are actually really common. If anything, it often signals that you're touching something meaningful. Your counselor won't judge you; they've seen it many times and their whole role is to support you through it.

You're allowed to feel whatever you feel there—that's the point of having a safe space. If it happens, you can simply let it happen, or even name it out loud ("I wasn't expecting to get emotional"). Try to be as gentle with yourself as you would with a friend in the same situation. Taking this step takes real courage, and the fact that you're going shows a lot of strength. I hope it goes well for you.

prompt: I've gone to a couple therapy sessions so far and still everytime I walk in I get nervous and shaky. Is this normal? Should I still be feeling like this?
response_text:
Yes, what you're feeling is completely normal. Therapy asks you to be vulnerable and open up about things that may be difficult, so it makes sense that your body responds with nervousness—even after a few sessions. Building trust and comfort with a new therapist often takes more than a couple of visits, and those shaky feelings usually ease over time as the relationship develops.

If it feels okay, consider mentioning this to your therapist directly. Naming the nervousness out loud can actually help lessen it, and a good therapist will welcome that honesty and can adjust the pace to help you feel more at ease. The fact that you keep showing up despite the nerves says a lot about your courage—give yourself credit for that.

prompt: I have been with my boyfriend for more than a year. He recently got a new job and travels a lot. I’m not used to him being gone all the time. I feel as though he has forgotten about me because he does not talk with me as much and doesn’t keep me up to date on everything that he does throughout the day, which he used to. I feel lost, sad and unwanted. This is really a tough new challenge. I just want to break up with him, but I love him so much. I don’t know why he is acting this way lately. I believe I have separation anxiety. Is there anything that I can do to help me cope with this while he is out of town?
response_text:
This is a really tough adjustment, and the sadness and loneliness you're feeling make complete sense. When someone's routine changes suddenly, it can feel like the connection itself is fading, even when love is still there. It's worth remembering that his reduced communication may have more to do with a demanding new schedule than his feelings for you.

A helpful first step might be an honest, gentle conversation—not to blame him, but to share how you feel and figure out a check-in rhythm that works for both of you, like a set call each evening. In the meantime, try leaning into things that ground you: friends, hobbies, movement, or anything that fills your days with meaning beyond the relationship. That can ease some of the anxious waiting.

Before deciding on a breakup while you're hurting, give yourself time to see how things settle. If these feelings become overwhelming, talking with a counselor could offer real support. You deserve reassurance and connection—it's okay to ask for it.

prompt: I had a head injury a few years ago and my mind races all the time. I have trouble sleeping and have a lot of anxiety. Every medicine I have been on my body rejects; I get sick to my stomach and get blisters in my mouth. How can I calm my self down? I'm a wreck.
response_text:
I'm really sorry you're dealing with this—racing thoughts, poor sleep, and constant anxiety are exhausting, especially when medications haven't been an option for you. That's a lot to carry, and it makes sense you feel like a wreck.

Since medicines have caused hard reactions, it's worth asking your doctor about non-medication approaches, and mentioning your head injury history—sometimes anxiety and sleep issues after a head injury need a specialized evaluation (like a neurologist). In the meantime, some people find slow breathing helpful: breathe in for four counts, hold briefly, then exhale slowly for six. Gentle movement, limiting screens before bed, and grounding techniques (naming things you can see, hear, and touch) can also ease a racing mind.

You don't have to figure this out alone. If your anxiety ever feels unbearable or you have thoughts of harming yourself, please reach out to a crisis line (call or text 988 in the US) right away. You deserve real support and relief.

prompt: I think I'm annoying and bothersome, but my girlfriend says I'm just fine. I don't think so, I think I'm stressing everyone else out
response_text:
It's really hard to carry that feeling that you're a burden to the people around you. That belief can be exhausting, and it often speaks louder than the reassurance others give you—even when someone who knows you well, like your girlfriend, tells you otherwise.

Here's something worth considering: the people in your life are showing you their honest response, and she's saying you're fine. That's real information, even if it's hard to trust right now. Feelings of being "annoying" often come from inside us rather than from how others actually see us. If this belief has been weighing on you for a while or making it hard to relax around people you care about, it might help to talk with a counselor who can help you unpack where it's coming from. You deserve to feel at ease with the people who want you around—and it sounds like they genuinely do.

prompt: How can I control my anxiety when I have Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder?
response_text:
Managing anxiety with OCD can feel exhausting, and it makes sense that you're looking for ways to cope. One of the most effective approaches for OCD is a form of therapy called Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP), which gently helps you face anxious thoughts without giving in to compulsions. Over time, this can reduce the grip anxiety has on you. If you're not already working with a mental health professional, connecting with one who specializes in OCD can make a real difference.

In the moment, grounding techniques may help—slow breathing, naming things you can see and hear, or reminding yourself that anxious thoughts are not facts and don't require action. Being patient and compassionate with yourself matters too; setbacks are part of the process, not failures.

If your anxiety ever feels overwhelming or you have thoughts of harming yourself, please reach out to a crisis line or emergency services right away. You don't have to manage this alone, and support is available.

prompt: I am extremely possessive in my relationships and this is hurting my friendships. How can I fix my underlying issues?
response_text:
It takes real self-awareness to notice this pattern and want to change it—that's an important first step.

Possessiveness often comes from underlying fears: of being abandoned, replaced, or not being enough. When those fears flare up, they can drive behaviors like jealousy, checking in constantly, or feeling threatened when friends have other relationships. A helpful place to start is getting curious about the moments it spikes. What thought or feeling comes right before? Often it's an insecurity looking for reassurance. Learning to notice that, pause, and remind yourself that your friends valuing others doesn't diminish your worth can slowly loosen the grip.

Building your own sense of self-worth outside of any single relationship also helps—hobbies, other connections, and things that make you feel capable. And if this feels rooted in deeper patterns, a therapist can help you explore where it comes from and build healthier ways of relating. Wanting to protect your friendships shows you care; that's something to build on.

prompt: I start to think of an issue that doesn't even matter or something bad that happened years ago. Then, I cry, pull at my hair, plug my ears, hit myself, and throw things. In loud public places, I get on edge and start being sarcastic and moody. I have an awful fear of people leaving me (which normally ends up happening) and I feel like I'm too clingy.
response_text:
It sounds like you're carrying a lot of intense emotions, and the way they surface—through hurting yourself, throwing things, and that deep fear of being left—must feel overwhelming and exhausting. What you're describing takes real courage to name, and I want you to know these reactions don't make you broken or "too much." They're signals that something inside you is hurting and looking for relief.

Because you mentioned hitting yourself and pulling your hair, I'd gently encourage you to reach out to a mental health professional who can help you understand what's driving these responses and build safer ways to cope. If the urge to hurt yourself ever feels hard to control, please contact a crisis line—in the US you can call or text 988 anytime.

You deserve support that doesn't leave. Talking to a counselor could be a steady starting point. Would it help to think through how to take that first step?

prompt: I am lazy. I am very aware of the problem and try to talk myself out of it all the time, but I never seem to shake the habits. I try to think of what it is doing to me and my future, but no matter what, I keep creating excuses for myself to continue the procrastination. All I'm ever left with is regrets and a low grade. I am at an all-time low in my life, and I'm not even that old. I've always been a straight-A student, but now I'm getting C's and F's, and it hurts me to know that I am way better than that. It's not even like the work is hard.
response_text:
What you're describing doesn't actually sound like laziness to me. A person who once earned straight A's and now can't get themselves to do easy work usually isn't lacking willpower—something else is often draining the fuel. Sudden drops in motivation, procrastination that won't budge no matter how hard you try, and feeling at an "all-time low" can be signs of burnout, depression, anxiety, or just being overwhelmed. Those things respond to support, not self-criticism.

Calling yourself lazy keeps you stuck in a shame loop, and shame rarely motivates. It might help to talk with a counselor at your school or a doctor to figure out what's really going on underneath this. In the meantime, try shrinking tasks down—commit to just five minutes on one thing, and let that be enough.

If you ever feel hopeless or like you can't go on, please reach out to a crisis line (988 in the US) or someone you trust. You clearly still care about your future—that matters.

prompt: I never get infections or scars or anything, and it doesn't bother me if it gets filled up with blood or something, but I'm concerned.
response_text:
It sounds like you're describing self-harm and noticing that certain things—infections, scars, bleeding—don't bother you the way you might expect. The fact that you say you're concerned matters a lot; part of you is paying attention and wants something different.

Even without infections or scars, hurting yourself can carry real risks, and it often points to pain that deserves care and support. You don't have to sort through this alone. Talking with a doctor or a mental health professional could help you understand what's going on and find other ways to cope. If you're in the US, you can call or text 988 anytime to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, or you can look up a local crisis line if you're elsewhere.

If you ever feel like you might seriously harm yourself, please reach out to emergency services or someone you trust right away. Would it help to think through who you could talk to first?

prompt: How do you know you have the right therapist for you? How would I know how to "train" my therapist to be able to give me what I need from treatment?
response_text:
Finding the right therapist often comes down to a few signs: you feel heard and respected, you can gradually be honest even about hard things, and you sense the relationship is safe enough to disagree or push back. It's also worth noticing whether you feel like you're making progress over time—though real change can be slow and uneven.

As for "training" your therapist, a good approach is direct communication rather than hoping they'll guess. You can say things like, "I need more structure," or "I'd like more feedback," or "That approach didn't land for me." A skilled therapist welcomes this and adjusts. If they seem defensive or dismissive when you share what you need, that itself is useful information. It can also help to name your goals early and revisit them together.

If after a fair try it still doesn't fit, it's okay to seek someone else—that's not failure, it's part of finding the right match.

prompt: Does counseling really do anything that can help people?
response_text:
That's a fair question, and it makes sense to wonder whether counseling is worth the time and effort. The honest answer is that research consistently shows therapy helps many people—reducing symptoms of depression and anxiety, improving relationships, and building coping skills. That said, it isn't magic, and results depend on things like the fit between you and the counselor, the type of approach used, and your own readiness to engage.

For a lot of people, the value comes from having a private space to be heard without judgment, along with practical tools to handle what's going on. If you try it and don't click with one counselor, it's okay to look for another—finding the right match matters. If you're considering it for something specific you're dealing with, it might help to start with even one session to see how it feels. What's making you curious about it right now?

prompt: How does a person start the counseling process?
response_text:
Starting counseling can feel intimidating, but the process is usually more straightforward than people expect. A good first step is to think about what you're hoping to work on—even a general sense like "I've been feeling anxious" is enough to begin. From there, you can find a counselor through your insurance provider's directory, your doctor's referral, a workplace employee assistance program (EAP), or online directories like Psychology Today, where you can filter by concern, location, and cost.

Once you find someone, you typically reach out by phone or email to schedule an initial session. Many therapists offer a brief free consultation to see if it's a good fit. That first appointment is mostly about getting to know each other—there's no pressure to have everything figured out. It's completely okay to try a few counselors before settling on one who feels right.

If cost is a barrier, community mental health centers and sliding-scale clinics can help. Taking that first step is often the hardest part, and reaching out shows real strength.

prompt: What are the basic skills a good counselor needs to have?
response_text:
A good counselor draws on several core skills. Active listening is fundamental—giving full attention, reflecting back what's said, and noticing tone and body language, not just words. Empathy allows them to understand a person's experience without judgment, while genuine warmth and respect help build trust and rapport.

Strong communication matters too: asking open questions, summarizing, and knowing when to stay silent. Counselors also need self-awareness to recognize their own biases and reactions, along with clear professional boundaries and ethics. Patience, cultural sensitivity, and the ability to stay calm during difficult moments round out the picture, as does knowing their limits and when to refer someone to other support.

If you're exploring this because you're considering becoming a counselor, that's a meaningful path—many of these skills grow with training and practice. If you're asking because you're looking for support yourself, I'm glad to talk more about what you're hoping to find.

prompt: What are some difficulties that a counselor can encounter when dealing with a client?
response_text:
Counselors often face a range of challenges in their work. One common difficulty is building trust, especially with clients who are guarded, ambivalent about being there, or have been let down by others in the past. Related to this is resistance—clients may struggle to open up, minimize their concerns, or feel unready to change even when they've sought help.

Other challenges include managing strong emotions in the room, recognizing when a client's needs fall outside their scope and require referral, and navigating ethical dilemmas like confidentiality limits or safety risks. Counselors also have to guard against burnout, countertransference (their own reactions getting stirred up), and cultural or communication differences that can affect rapport.

If you're asking because you're training or working in this field, ongoing supervision and peer support can be really valuable for working through these situations. Is there a particular difficulty you're trying to navigate right now? I'm happy to explore it further with you.

prompt: My last relationships have ended horribly. They just up and abandoned me. One of them I have never gotten closure with over it, leaving me emotionally wrecked. I know something's wrong with me but I don't know how to even start trying to better myself. I get into these depressed like states whenever anyone I care about is too busy to be with me. I know that I shouldn't act like that because people are genuinely busy, but I feel like they're doing it just because they don't want to be around me.
response_text:
It takes real courage to look honestly at your patterns like this, and the fact that you want to understand yourself better is genuinely a strong starting point—not a sign that something is fundamentally "wrong" with you.

What you're describing—the fear of abandonment, the pain when people are busy, the ache of unresolved endings—makes a lot of sense given what you've been through. Those old wounds can make your mind interpret ordinary distance as rejection, even when it isn't. That's not a character flaw; it's a protective response that can be understood and softened over time.

You don't have to fix everything at once. A helpful first step might be talking with a therapist who can help you make sense of these reactions and build tools to feel steadier. If cost is a barrier, community mental health centers or sliding-scale options can help.

Be gentle with yourself as you start. Wanting closeness isn't wrong—you deserve support in finding it in ways that feel safe.

prompt: I just feel sad all the time and I don't like anyone in my family. I feel like they're trying to control me and won't let me grow.
response_text:
It sounds really heavy to feel sad so constantly, and to feel like the people around you are holding you back instead of helping you grow. That kind of tension at home can be exhausting, especially when you're trying to figure out who you are.

Wanting more independence is a normal and healthy part of growing up, and it doesn't make you a bad person for feeling frustrated with your family. Sometimes what feels like control is fear or worry on their part, but that doesn't make your need for space any less valid. If you feel able, it might help to talk with someone you trust—a counselor, teacher, or another supportive adult—about what you're going through. And if the sadness ever feels overwhelming or you have thoughts of hurting yourself, please reach out to a crisis line or someone nearby right away. You deserve support, and your feelings matter.

prompt: I self-harm, and I stop for awhile. Then when I see something sad or depressing, I automatically want to self-harm.
response_text:
It makes a lot of sense that this feels frustrating—you work hard to stop, and then something painful hits and the urge comes rushing back. That doesn't mean you've failed; it means the urge got linked to strong emotions, and that connection can be gently retrained over time.

When you notice that pull after seeing something sad, try to pause and name what you're feeling, then reach for something that gives a similar intense sensation without harm—gripping ice, a cold shower, snapping a rubber band, or intense exercise. Building a short list of things to do in those moments can help you ride out the wave, since urges usually peak and fade.

You deserve support with this, not just white-knuckling it alone. Talking to a counselor or therapist can help you work through what's underneath these urges. And if you ever feel you might seriously hurt yourself, please reach out right away—call or text 988 (US) or your local crisis line. You're not alone in this.

prompt: I'm depressed. I have been for years. I hide it from everyone because I'm scared of the reactions I'll get. Last time I tried telling my parents, it was a huge argument about me being too young to be depressed (I’m a legal adult), calling me ungrateful, and telling me that if I can't handle things now, it's only going to get worse in the future (which is turning out to be true). It's exhausting pretending to be okay, and I don't know how much longer I can try. I'm just really tired, and sadly, I can't afford the help I need on my own.
response_text:
I'm really glad you reached out here, and I want you to know that carrying this alone for years while pretending everything's fine takes enormous strength. It makes sense that you're exhausted. Your depression is real and valid, regardless of your age, and the way your parents responded doesn't reflect the truth about you—it reflects their own limits in understanding.

When you say you don't know how much longer you can try, I want to gently check in: if you're having thoughts of harming yourself or not being here, please reach out to a crisis line right now. In the US you can call or text 988, or text HOME to 741741—both are free and confidential.

For ongoing support that fits a tight budget, low-cost options exist: sliding-scale clinics, community mental health centers, and services like Open Path Collective. You deserve help, and needing it isn't a weakness. You don't have to keep holding all of this by yourself.

prompt: He said he would try and he never did. It's been nine months, and this is making me worse. Today, he said I have to respect whatever decision he makes. Is that true? Am I supposed to respect the decision to leave because he can't handle what I'm going through and leaves me here crying and worried every night? He's constantly changing his mind on if he wants to work it out.
response_text:
That sounds incredibly painful, and it makes complete sense that months of broken promises and mixed signals have worn you down. Being told to "respect his decision" while he keeps changing his mind isn't really respect at all—it's leaving you carrying all the uncertainty and hurt on your own.

You can respect that a person has the right to make their own choices, but that doesn't mean you have to accept being kept in limbo or blamed for struggling while you're not being supported. Your feelings are valid, and needing stability and honesty isn't asking too much.

You deserve care, not to cry alone every night. If the worry ever becomes overwhelming or you feel unsafe with your own thoughts, please reach out to a crisis line or someone you trust. And talking with a counselor could help you sort through what you truly want and need going forward. You matter here.

prompt: Every time my partner gets angry for anything, she takes it out on me. Nothing I do is right, and once she's mad, she calls me all kinds of names and is verbally abusive. She says it isn’t abuse, it’s just angry verbal bashing, and that it’s different. It gets worse each time. The names are very vulgar now.
response_text:
What you're describing—being called vulgar names, having everything you do treated as wrong, and this escalating over time—is verbal abuse, regardless of what it's labeled. Calling it "angry verbal bashing" doesn't change the impact it's having on you. You deserve to be treated with respect, especially by someone who's supposed to care about you.

It's not your fault that she gets angry, and no amount of "doing things right" will prevent someone else's choice to lash out. That pattern of escalation is worth taking seriously. You might consider talking with a therapist or contacting a domestic violence support line (in the US, 1-800-799-7233), which also assists with verbal and emotional abuse and can help you think through your situation confidentially.

If things ever feel physically unsafe, please reach out to emergency services or someone you trust right away. You don't have to carry this alone.

prompt: My friend’s husband is bipolar and refuses to take medication for it. He has taken the wheels off her vehicle before to prevent her from leaving. He has held her a prisoner in her home. He has choked her, hit her, etc. She has almost divorced him a couple of times but always makes up with him, thinking that he is going to change. She and I went to a wedding out of town in September of 2014, and ever since she has been back, he is convinced that she cheated on him while we were gone. Now he is saying that I have also cheated on my boyfriend and has come to my house and told my boyfriend this.
response_text:
What you're describing about your friend's situation is serious—choking, hitting, holding her prisoner, and disabling her vehicle are forms of domestic violence, and they can escalate. It's understandable that you're worried, especially now that his behavior is spilling over onto you and your own relationship.

You can't force your friend to leave, but you can keep offering her a safe, non-judgmental connection so she knows she isn't alone. It may help to have the National Domestic Violence Hotline handy for both of you: 1-800-799-7233 (or text START to 88788). They can advise on safety planning even when someone isn't ready to leave.

For yourself, take his showing up at your home seriously—consider documenting these incidents and talking with your boyfriend openly. If you ever feel physically threatened by him, don't hesitate to call 911. Your safety matters too, not just your friend's.

prompt: After a domestic abuse situation, I went to a therapist, and then my husband went. The therapist discussed her assessment of borderline personality disorder with me. She then told my abuser the results of my tests.
response_text:
I'm so sorry this happened. What you're describing is a serious breach of confidentiality and professional ethics—your therapist should not have shared your assessment results with anyone, especially the person who harmed you. That betrayal on top of an abusive situation is a lot to carry, and your anger or hurt about it is completely valid.

A few things you might consider: you have the right to file a complaint with your therapist's licensing board, and you can request a copy of your own records. You may also want to find a new therapist—ideally one experienced with domestic abuse and trauma—who can support you safely.

Please also make sure your immediate safety is protected. If you're in danger, you can reach the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233 (24/7) or text START to 88788. If you're ever in immediate danger, call 911.

You deserved better than this. What happened was not your fault.

prompt: I've been with my boyfriend over 3 years. He cheated on me and the woman is now pregnant. He is physically and mentally abusive towards me. I have attempted to talk with him in order to resolve our issues; however, he never wants to talk and often blames me for everything. I’m always there when he needs my help. He tells me although I help him doesn’t mean that I am a good person. He always discredits me as a woman and it’s hurtful. I spend most day crying and feeling lonely. I am unhappy and unsure of what I need to do.
response_text:
I'm so sorry you're carrying this much pain. What you're describing—physical and emotional abuse, betrayal, being blamed and torn down—is not something you caused, and it's not something you deserve. The way he treats you is not a reflection of your worth. You sound like someone who gives a lot, and it hurts deeply to have that met with cruelty.

Please know your safety matters most. Physical abuse can escalate, and you don't have to face this alone. If you're in the US, you can reach the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233 (or text START to 88788) any time, confidentially—they can help you think through your options and safety, without pressure. If you're ever in immediate danger, call emergency services.

You mentioned crying most days and feeling unsure and alone—those feelings make sense given what you're living through. Is there a trusted friend or family member you could lean on right now? You deserve support and to feel safe.

prompt: Now I have anger and trust issues. How can I treat this and fix myself?
response_text:
It takes real strength to recognize these patterns and want to work on them—so first, please know that wanting to grow doesn't mean you're broken. Anger and trust difficulties often develop as protective responses to painful experiences, and they can absolutely soften with time and effort.

A good starting point is noticing what triggers these feelings and pausing before reacting—even a few slow breaths or stepping away can help. Journaling about what you're feeling and where it might come from can bring clarity, and rebuilding trust often works best in small, low-risk steps with people who've earned it. prompt: Can a therapist have a client admitted to an eating disorder treatment center if the client does not want to go?

prompt: I have a problem with binge eating, especially during times of stress. prompt: I don’t love my sister. I would never wish her harm, but if I could, I would wish for us not to be related. Is this cruel? Why must blood mean we have to be friends? prompt: My mother takes care of niece whom my sister abandoned. She calls me every day complaining, but I don't want to hear it anymore.

prompt: How do I overcome being jealous of my boyfriends mother?

prompt: I just lost my grandpa and i'm having a rough time with it. I need some help to deal with the loss, but I don’t think I can pay for counseling. Where Can I get help?

prompt: How do I deal with the pain of losing my baby?

prompt: Can a past therapist disclose information to a current therapist that you are seeing?
response_text:
Generally, no—not without your permission. Therapists are bound by confidentiality rules (like HIPAA in the U.S.), so a past therapist cannot share your information with a current one unless you provide written consent, usually through a signed release-of-information form.

If you'd like your two therapists to coordinate care, you can request that yourself, and you get to decide what information is shared. There are limited exceptions where disclosure may happen without consent—such as a serious safety risk or a legal requirement—but routine sharing between providers requires your authorization. If you have concerns about your specific situation, it's worth asking your current therapist directly about their confidentiality policies. They should be able to walk you through your options and rights.

prompt: I terminated my counseling relationship with a social worker several years ago. I am now realizing that I would like to begin counseling again. prompt: My ex-wife married and used me to have a child. She now uses that child as a pawn. I know my child misses me, but I need to move on and not live in the past. How do I do this? Do I see my child as much as possible or very little? Is it more confusing for the child?

prompt: Can a counselor take sides with one parent and allow a parent to order the child to tell the counselor "every detail" about what happened during the other parent’s visitation in order to help build a case for child custody?

That kind of pressure can weigh heavily on a parent, especially when finances are tight and you have four children to think about.

Being honest with her about what's realistic right now is not a failure—it's part of a healthy adult relationship. If you'd like, it may help to talk openly with her about the situation together, so the responsibility doesn't feel like it rests only on you.

Is there a particular part of this that's troubling you most? I'm happy to listen.

prompt: I am divorced and happily remarried. Our blended family of children are in their 20s. My youngest, age 20, continues to call me crazy and favors her dad. prompt: How does a counselor decide when to end counseling sessions or to terminate working with a client?
response_text:
Counselors typically consider ending or transitioning care when a few things line up. The most common reason is progress: when you've met the goals you set together, developed coping skills, and feel more equipped to handle challenges on your own, that's often a natural point to wrap up. Termination is ideally a collaborative decision, discussed openly rather than announced suddenly.

There are other reasons too. A counselor might refer you elsewhere if your needs fall outside their area of expertise, if a different level of care would serve you better, or if there's a conflict of interest. Practical factors like a move, insurance changes, or scheduling can also play a role. Ethical guidelines encourage counselors to avoid abandoning clients, so good practice includes giving notice, reviewing what you've accomplished, and helping arrange next steps if needed.

If you're wondering about your own counseling, it's completely appropriate to ask your counselor directly how they think about it—that conversation is part of the work.

prompt: My therapist is gay so there are no sexual issues here. However, my therapist for six years has made me believe that he cares about me and that we are friends. I have loaned money to him many times, and he always paid me back. I had a medical emergency last weekend and I was heavily medicated. I knew that this therapist came into my home and wrote down my credit card information so he could pay back what he owed me, but this therapist dropped me off and never came again. I don't know what to do.
response_text:
This sounds deeply confusing and painful, especially coming from someone you trusted for six years. What you're describing raises serious concerns about professional boundaries—therapists borrowing money from clients, entering your home, and accessing your financial information all fall well outside ethical practice, regardless of how the relationship felt.

First, please check your credit card and bank accounts right away for any unauthorized charges, and consider contacting your card company if anything looks wrong. It may also help to write down what you remember while it's fresh. You have the right to file a complaint with your state's licensing board, which handles exactly these kinds of ethical violations. If you feel unsafe or believe a crime occurred, contacting local authorities is reasonable too.

You deserve care that keeps you safe, not one that blurs into loans and confusion. Please also think about reaching out to a trusted friend or family member so you're not carrying this alone. You didn't do anything wrong here.

prompt: I just wanted to get to know one so I can hear about their college experience and the courses they took. I also wanted to know if they enjoy their job and how long they were in school.
response_text:

Most people are happy to share their experience when asked genuinely. When you talk with them, feel free to ask exactly what you mentioned—their courses, how long they studied, and whether they enjoy the work day to day. Would it help to think through who you might reach out to first?

prompt: I am an international student, and it is my first semester in graduate school in the United States. I faced a cultural shock, and I was so depressed when I arrived here. response_text:

Wine in particular can be complicated. A safer choice might be something meaningful but non-alcoholic that represents your country, or simply a heartfelt thank-you card or note describing how much his help meant to you. Honestly, sincere words often mean more than any object.

If you'd still like to give something, you could ask him directly whether he's allowed to accept a small token—that way you avoid putting him in an awkward position. Enjoy your vacation, and be proud of how far you've come this semester.

prompt: I'm worried I should see a therapist due to past events and current mental status. I'm just so unsure of how to ask my doctor about seeing someone.
response_text:
It's completely understandable to feel unsure—many people find this a hard conversation to start, and the fact that you're considering it shows real self-awareness and courage.

You don't need the perfect words. You could simply say something like, "I've been struggling with some things from my past and how I'm feeling lately, and I think I'd benefit from talking to a therapist. Can you help me find a referral?" If saying it out loud feels tough, you can write it down and hand your doctor a note, or ask for a mental health check-in when you book the appointment. Your doctor deals with these requests regularly, so you don't have to explain everything perfectly.

If your symptoms ever feel overwhelming or you have thoughts of harming yourself, please reach out to a crisis line or emergency services right away. You deserve support, and taking this step is a meaningful one.

prompt: I'm obsessing about a terrible breakup. Everything is a constant reminder. How do I move on?
response_text:
Breakups can feel all-consuming, and it makes sense that everything around you seems to point back to that pain. The mind tends to loop on what we've lost, especially when reminders are everywhere. Please be gentle with yourself—healing from this isn't a switch you flip, it's a gradual process, and obsessive thoughts are a normal part of grief.

A few things can help: try gently redirecting your attention when the thoughts spiral, rather than fighting them, and give yourself permission to feel the sadness without judging it. Small changes to your environment—rearranging a room, taking new routes, filling time with people or activities that ground you—can ease the constant triggers. Writing down your thoughts sometimes releases some of their grip too.

If the obsessing feels unmanageable or starts affecting your sleep, eating, or daily functioning, talking with a therapist could really help you work through it. You won't feel this intensely forever, even though it's hard to believe right now.

prompt: I know that I need to get past my feelings for this person I fell in love with, but t's so difficult to move on because he showed me feelings I've never felt before. I feel like I don't want to be without my genuine love for him, but logically, I know I need to be without him. I can't discuss this with anybody in my life because the conditions surrounding our love are considered "wrong" by a lot of people. How can I get myself to just move on?
response_text:
It makes sense that this feels so hard. When someone opens up feelings in us we've never experienced before, letting go isn't just about the person—it's about grieving a part of ourselves that came alive with them. That's a real loss, and it deserves patience rather than pressure to "just move on."

You don't have to force yourself to stop caring; that genuine love was real, and honoring it isn't the same as staying attached. Moving on tends to happen gradually as you build a life full enough that the space he occupied slowly fills with other meaningful things. And carrying this alone, especially when you fear judgment, adds another layer of pain. A therapist offers a completely confidential, non-judgmental space where you could talk through the details you can't share elsewhere—that might ease some of the isolation. You deserve support with this, not shame. Be gentle with yourself; healing from something this significant takes time.

prompt: My wife just last week said she wants a divorce and it's all sudden. I understand that marriages have their ups and downs but I don't understand why she can't tell me why she wants a divorce. Should I fight for my family (daughter and wife)?
response_text:
I can hear how blindsided and hurt you are right now—a sudden request like this, without a clear reason, leaves you grasping for answers and understandably wanting to hold your family together. That confusion is painful.

Whether to "fight" isn't really the question so much as how you show up. You can express that you want to understand and work on things, and calmly ask her for honest conversation—maybe through couples counseling if she's open to it. But you can't force her to stay or to explain before she's ready, and pushing hard can sometimes deepen the distance. Focus on what you can control: staying present and steady for your daughter, taking care of yourself, and communicating without pressure.

It may also help to talk to a counselor or a trusted friend for your own support through this, and eventually to understand your options. Whatever happens with your marriage, your role as a father remains. Be gentle with yourself right now.

prompt: I keep on begging him to come back. I am so unhappy with him but am so scared of being a single parent to our son. I was abused as a little girl and that has made to be very abusive to men. What should I do...
response_text:
It sounds like you're carrying so much pain right now—the fear of parenting alone, the hurt from what happened to you as a child, and the exhaustion of a relationship that isn't making you happy. That's a heavy load, and it makes sense you feel torn.

A few things stand out. Begging someone to stay in a relationship where you're unhappy often keeps you stuck without meeting your real needs. And the childhood abuse you mentioned deserves care and healing on its own—working with a trauma-informed therapist could help you understand these patterns and treat yourself and others differently.

You don't have to figure this out all at once. If you or your son are ever in danger, please reach out to a domestic violence hotline or emergency services. Otherwise, consider talking to a counselor who can help you sort through your fears about single parenting and what you truly want. You deserve support in this.

prompt: How do couples keep from being at risk for divorce?
response_text:
Great question—strong relationships take intentional effort over time. A few things tend to make a real difference: keeping communication open and honest, especially about the hard topics like money, intimacy, and expectations. Couples who do well often learn to argue fairly—focusing on the issue rather than attacking each other, and taking breaks when things get heated. Showing appreciation regularly and making time for connection, even in small ways, helps couples stay emotionally close rather than drifting into just "roommates."

It also helps to keep growing together, supporting each other's individual goals while building shared ones. When bigger struggles come up, seeking help early—like couples counseling—can prevent small problems from becoming large ones. Reaching out isn't a sign of failure; it's a sign you value the relationship.

If you're asking because something specific is weighing on you or your partner right now, I'm glad to talk through it more. What's on your mind?

prompt: We've been in a long distance relationship for two and a half years. I recently saw his phone and saw the people he texts the most and one of them was a female coworker. I don't know how to approach this situation. How do I ask him about it?.

It's understandable to feel unsettled by this, especially when distance already makes it harder to feel connected. When you bring it up, try leading with honesty and curiosity rather than accusation. You might say something like, "I noticed you text a coworker pretty often, and I felt a little unsure about it. Can you tell me about your friendship with her?" Framing it around your feelings ("I felt") rather than blame tends to keep the conversation open instead of defensive. Pay attention to how he responds—openness and reassurance are good signs, while defensiveness or secrecy might be worth exploring further.

It's also worth reflecting on what's driving the worry: is it this specific situation, or a deeper need for security in the relationship? Both are valid things to talk through together.

prompt: I’ve been in a long distance relationship with my girlfriend for just over a year. This past week she admitted to me that she has feelings for another guy. She says it’s “just a crush” but I don't know how to cope with it. How should I deal with this?

Give yourself permission to feel hurt without rushing to a decision. Leaning on a trusted friend or writing out your thoughts can ease some of the weight while you figure out what feels right for you.

prompt: However, it seems as though he is really talking to someone other than himself. I have even accused him of having a secret phone. Is he trying to make me crazy on purpose, or is he really talking to himself?

If you find yourself doubting your own perceptions or feeling like you're being made to feel "crazy," that's worth paying attention to. Talking it through with a trusted friend or a counselor could help you sort out what's real and what you need.

prompt: I'm in a relationship with my fiancé and I currently found out that she's been cheating on me with a co-worker. I was very upset none the less. response_text:
I'm sorry you're carrying this pain. What you're feeling—the constant intrusive images, the unsettled heart, the desire to hold onto a life you've built together—all of that makes sense. Nine years and a child give you real reasons to want to heal this, and your willingness to forgive shows how much you love her.

At the same time, moving forward doesn't mean pretending it didn't happen. Rebuilding trust after betrayal usually takes honest conversations about why it happened, what both of you need now, and rebuilding safety over time. prompt: We’ve been together almost three years. We argue and he ends it by telling me he doesn’t love me. response_text:
It makes sense that this hurts—being told "I don't love you" during arguments cuts deep, and you're carrying a lot by apologizing and dropping things just to keep the peace. That kind of one-sided repair can leave you feeling unseen, even when you're the one working hardest to resolve things.

One thing to notice: real resolution takes both people. You can't communicate for both of you, and swallowing your pride every time may keep things quiet without actually healing the pattern. It might help to talk with him during a calm moment—not mid-argument—about how those words land on you and what you both need. Couples counseling can be genuinely useful here, giving you tools and a neutral space to be heard.

Wanting to keep your family intact is understandable, but you also deserve a relationship where love isn't used as a weapon. What would feel like a supportive first step for you?

prompt: I'm always told I'm not good enough or trying hard enough. I put 100% in to every thing. response_text:
It sounds like you're pouring everything you have into being your best self—your relationships, your studies, your kindness, your values—and still hearing that it isn't enough. One hard truth: sometimes no amount of effort will satisfy certain people, and their reaction may say more about them than about you. Your worth isn't determined by whether they're impressed. It might help to notice whose voice that "not good enough" belief comes from, and to start building your own measure of when you've done well.

If this hopelessness ever deepens or you have thoughts of harming yourself, please reach out to someone you trust or a crisis line (in the US, call or text 988). You've clearly got strength—please don't carry this entirely alone.

prompt: It's been almost a year since my ex-boyfriend broke up with me after he cheated on me many times. response_text:
What you're carrying sounds so heavy, and it makes complete sense that this betrayal still hurts. Watching your father cheat and grow up around alcoholism can leave a deep imprint, shaping how much you seek validation and fear abandonment. You don't have to choose between forgiveness and hate, both can coexist. You can be grateful for the money he lent and still be angry about the cheating. Both feelings are valid. The obsessive checking is often how our mind tries to regain control over something painful, but it keeps the wound raw. Muting or unfollowing him might give you breathing room.

Given the nightmares and how this haunts you day and night, talking with a therapist could really help you untangle these older roots. You deserve that support.

prompt: I'm a male in my 20s. My girlfriend is in her late 30s. She's great. She's funny and smart, she has a big heart, and we have an excellent sex life. response_text:
It sounds like you care about her deeply, and that care is getting tangled up with fear and self-doubt. Before making a big decision out of fear, it might help to talk honestly with her about how you're feeling, including the guilt about her housing situation. You may be assuming things about her happiness that she doesn't feel. And if the trust issues run deep, a therapist could help you understand where they come from and build more security—for your sake, not just the relationship's.

You don't have to solve everything tonight. Try one honest conversation, and consider getting some support for yourself. What feels like being trapped might actually be a decision you're allowed to make slowly.

prompt: About 3 years ago or so I was skinny, but I was still ugly. I really do want to change that but I've tried 3 times. Now can I try but don't stop. prompt: Everyone around me is much smarter and flaunts it. Everyone around me is skinny, and here I am trying to throw up so I'm not fat. prompt: These "jokes" are made about everything. They seem to have the need to say something "funny" about everything. It's not funny, just awkward.
response_text:
It sounds really draining to be around someone who turns everything into a joke, especially when it lands as awkward instead of funny. That constant need to comment can leave you feeling like nothing is taken seriously, and that's a valid frustration.

If this is a person you interact with regularly, it might help to name what you're noticing—something simple like, "I know you mean it lightly, but sometimes I'd rather we just talk normally." What is it about the joking that bothers you most—is it the timing, the topics, or feeling like you can't have a genuine moment?

prompt: It's really hard to not have negative feelings about friends who don't put any effort into nourishing our relationship.
response_text:
It makes complete sense that you'd feel hurt or frustrated when friendship feels one-sided. Wanting effort in return isn't demanding—it's a reasonable hope for connection, and noticing that imbalance shows how much you value closeness.

Sometimes it helps to gently name what you need, either to yourself or directly to a friend, and see how they respond. Their reaction can tell you a lot about where to invest your energy. It's also okay to let some relationships become lighter while giving your attention to people who show up for you. Your negative feelings aren't a flaw; they're information about what matters to you. Be kind to yourself as you figure out what feels right.

prompt: I was “mentored” by this guy for a few years spiritually. It was okay at times, but other times, it was just weird. response_text:
What you're describing sounds really painful and disorienting—especially the experience of not being believed and being blamed for problems that weren't yours to carry. prompt: I would like to be able to have more positive relationships in the present.
response_text:
That's a really meaningful goal, and wanting more positive connection speaks well of you. Building healthier relationships often starts with small, intentional steps rather than a big overhaul.

A few things can help: try being present and curious with the people you're already around—asking questions and really listening builds closeness over time. Being open about who you are, even in small ways, invites others to connect more genuinely with you.

If this feels tied to deeper struggles or feels hard to move forward on alone, talking with a counselor can be a supportive place to work through it. What kind of relationships would you most like to grow right now?

prompt: They're calling me names like hypocrite and a baby even when they act in the same manner as I do. I'm tired of being called names. What should I do?
response_text:
Being called names repeatedly is exhausting and hurtful, and it makes sense that you're tired of it. It's especially frustrating when the people criticizing you act the same way—that double standard isn't fair to you.

You don't have to accept name-calling. You can calmly set a boundary, like saying, "I'm not okay with being called that, so I'm going to step away if it continues," and then actually removing yourself from the conversation when it happens. You can't control how others behave, but you can control how much you let their words define you—their name-calling reflects them, not your worth. If this is coming from people you're around a lot, it may help to talk it through with someone you trust who can support you. Do you have anyone like that in your life right now?

prompt: My brother has been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia and has not been taking his medication. He's been using methamphetamine and alcohol and was found sleeping naked in my step mom driveway in 12 degree weather. I was adopted in by his dad (who just passed) and his mother will not Get involved because she's afraid of financial responsibility. Do I have the rights to be able to sign my brother into mentalhealth facility?
response_text:
I'm so sorry you're carrying this while also grieving your father's death. What you're describing sounds frightening and exhausting, and your care for your brother really comes through.

To answer your question directly: whether you can have him committed depends on your state's laws and your legal relationship to him. Most states allow involuntary psychiatric holds (often 72 hours) when someone is a danger to themselves or others due to mental illness—and sleeping naked in freezing weather may qualify. You usually don't need to be a specific relative to start this; you can call a mobile crisis team, 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lineup), or in an emergency, 911, and report that he's endangering himself. For longer-term guardianship or commitment, you'd typically petition a court, and it helps to speak with a local attorney or your county mental health department.

If he's in immediate danger from the cold or substances, please call 911 now. You don't have to figure this out alone.

prompt: I'm a female in my mid 20s. Lately I tend to over drink and I've become a very angry drunk. In the past, I have even cheated on my boyfriend while I was under the influence of alcohol. prompt: Or how to send him somewhere that can help him, something like The Baker Act.

You generally can't file it yourself, but you can help set it in motion. If there's an immediate emergency or he's in danger, call 911 and tell them your concerns—law enforcement can initiate an evaluation. You can also contact a physician, mental health professional, or a mobile crisis team in your area. If you can share what state you're in, the process may differ, so local crisis resources are your best bet. You don't have to figure this out alone.

prompt: My new daughter-in-law just informed me that she is smoking marijuana while pregnant because of her morning sickness. I’m in shock and I don’t know how to respond. I just lost my mom, and she was good with advice.
response_text:
I'm so sorry for the loss of your mom—that grief on top of this worry must feel overwhelming, especially when she was the person you'd normally turn to.

It makes sense you're shaken. This is a genuine concern, and there's good reason for it: major health organizations advise against marijuana during pregnancy because it may affect fetal development. That said, how you respond matters as much as what you say. Coming at her with alarm may make her defensive, while curiosity and care may keep the door open. You might gently say you understand morning sickness is miserable and ask if she's talked with her OB about safe options—many doctors can suggest alternatives.

Ultimately this is her and your son's decision, and you may not be able to control the outcome, only offer your perspective with love. If it helps, you could encourage her to bring it up with her provider directly. Be gentle with yourself, too—you're navigating a lot right now.

prompt: I am a survivor of multiple sexual abuse/rape experiences. Triggers are having an effect on my daily life and my sexual relationship with my partner. I'm trying to learn to cope with them.
response_text:
Thank you for sharing something so personal—it takes real courage to speak about this, and I want to acknowledge how much you've endured. The fact that you're actively working to cope shows strength, even when it doesn't feel that way.

Triggers affecting your daily life and intimacy are a very understandable response to trauma, not a personal failing. Many survivors find that working with a therapist who specializes in trauma—especially approaches like EMDR or trauma-focused therapy—can help make triggers feel more manageable over time. Grounding techniques, like focusing on your breath or naming things you can see and touch, can also help in the moment when you feel activated.

If you haven't already, gently sharing with your partner what feels safe and what doesn't can ease pressure around intimacy, and moving at your own pace is completely valid. If you ever feel overwhelmed or unsafe, please reach out to a crisis line like RAINN (1-800-656-4673). You deserve support and care.

prompt: I recently lost a friend to suicide. I'm smoking marijuana and drinking more to cope with it. How can I handle this better?
response_text:

Using substances to numb the pain is a very human response, but it can make grief harder to move through over time. Some gentler ways to cope might be talking with someone you trust, letting yourself feel and express the grief, and keeping small routines like eating, sleeping, and moving your body. Grief support groups—especially those for suicide loss, like survivors of suicide loss groups—can help you feel less alone with feelings others may not understand.

If you find the drinking or smoking hard to cut back on, or if you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, please reach out to a doctor, counselor, or a crisis line (in the US, call or text 988). You deserve support through this.

prompt: I have been diagnosed with posttraumatic stress disorder due to my military experiences. Not a year ago, I had a car accident. Could this experience add more problems?

prompt: How can I get therapy for posttraumatic stress disorder without any money or insurance?
response_text:
There are real options for accessing PTSD treatment even without money or insurance. Community mental health centers often offer services on a sliding scale based on income, sometimes as low as a few dollars or free. You can find these by searching your area or calling 211 (in the U.S.), which connects you to local resources.

Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) provide care regardless of ability to pay. University training clinics offer low-cost therapy from supervised graduate students, and some therapists in private practice reserve pro bono or reduced-fee slots. If your trauma is related to military service, the VA has trauma programs. Nonprofits like Open Path Collective offer sessions at reduced rates, and warmlines or trauma-focused support groups can help in the meantime.

If you ever feel unsafe or in crisis, please reach out to 988 (Suicide and Crisis Lifeline) by call or text. You deserve support, and taking this step to seek help matters.

prompt: As a child, my parents injured my brother, so they went to prison. I was there when he had gotten hurt, but I can't seem to remember. I also can't remember being with them quite well. It's a blur.

prompt: I am in a high stress position for a tech company. I am being overworked and underpaid for my contributions and it is not only giving me anxiety, but also demoralizing. What can I do to manage my stress?

For the anxiety itself, practices like paced breathing or brief mindfulness can settle your nervous system in the moment. Longer term, it's worth naming the root problem: the mismatch between your contributions and your compensation. Consider documenting your accomplishments and having a direct conversation with your manager about workload and pay, or quietly exploring whether other roles might value you more fairly. You deserve to be compensated for what you bring.

If the stress starts affecting your sleep, health, or sense of hope more seriously, talking with a therapist can give you real support. You don't have to carry this alone.
